v.q: You write a custom annotation and a framework never sees it at run time. What is the most likely mistake?
o: The annotation is missing @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
The annotation has no elements with default values
The annotation was placed on a private field
The annotation interface was not declared as final
v.w: The default retention is CLASS, so the annotation is in the class file but not readable by reflection. RUNTIME is needed for frameworks.

v.q: Which statement about annotation retention is NOT true?
o: SOURCE annotations can be read through reflection at run time
The default retention is CLASS
RUNTIME annotations are stored in the class file
SOURCE annotations are dropped by the compiler
v.w: SOURCE annotations vanish after compiling, so reflection never sees them. Only RUNTIME ones are readable while the program runs.

o: All methods declared by that class, including private ones, but not inherited ones
All public methods of the class, including inherited ones
Only the methods annotated with a RUNTIME annotation
All methods of the class and of every superclass
v.w: getMethods() is the public and inherited set. getDeclaredMethods() is every method declared by this class only, whatever its visibility.

v.q: Which call returns only the public methods of a class, including those it inherits?
o: getMethods()
getDeclaredMethods()
getEnclosingMethod()
getDeclaredConstructors()
v.w: getMethods() is the public and inherited set. getDeclaredMethods() is every method this class declares, whatever its visibility, but not inherited ones.

v.q: A method called through Method.invoke throws an IllegalStateException. What does the caller of invoke receive?
o: An InvocationTargetException whose cause is the IllegalStateException
The IllegalStateException itself, unchanged
An IllegalAccessException describing the failed call
A RuntimeException with no cause attached
v.w: invoke wraps exceptions from the target method. Call getCause() to get the real one, and unwrap it in proxy handlers.

v.q: Which statement about InvocationTargetException is NOT true?
o: It is thrown when the Method object itself cannot be found
It wraps an exception thrown by the invoked method
getCause() returns the real exception
Proxy handlers usually unwrap it and rethrow the cause
v.w: It comes from Method.invoke, not from the lookup. A missing method gives NoSuchMethodException instead.

v.q: Why can a JDK dynamic proxy only be created for interfaces?
o: The generated class already extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and Java has single inheritance
Class files cannot be generated at run time for ordinary classes
Interfaces are the only types the class loader can load twice
Methods of a class cannot be called through an InvocationHandler
v.w: The proxy class extends Proxy, so it cannot also extend your class. CGLIB and ByteBuddy generate a subclass instead.

v.q: A proxy created with Proxy.newProxyInstance is cast to the implementation class AccountImpl and fails. Why?
o: The proxy implements the interface only and is not an AccountImpl
The proxy was created for a final class
The InvocationHandler was not registered with the class loader
Casts are not allowed on objects created by reflection
v.w: A JDK proxy is a generated class that extends Proxy and implements the interfaces. It is never an instance of the target class, so depend on the interface.

v.q: Why is @Transactional ignored on a final method of a Spring bean proxied by CGLIB?
o: A subclass proxy cannot override a final method, so the call skips the advice
Final methods are always run in a new thread by the JVM
Spring only reads annotations that are on interface methods
The JVM removes annotations from final methods at load time
v.w: A CGLIB proxy works by overriding methods. A final method cannot be overridden, and a private one is not visible, so no advice runs.

v.q: Which situation is NOT a reason why a Spring bean method fails to run its @Transactional advice?
o: The method is public and called from another bean
The method is final and the bean is proxied by CGLIB
The method is private
The bean calls the method on this
v.w: A public method called through the injected proxy is the normal, working case. Final, private and self-invoked methods all skip the proxy.

v.q: What is the difference between an annotation processor and reflection?
o: A processor runs at compile time and generates code, whereas reflection works on loaded classes at run time
A processor runs when the application starts, and reflection runs at compile time
A processor can only read annotations, and reflection can only read methods
They are two names for the same mechanism in different JDK versions
v.w: MapStruct and Dagger generate code during compilation, with no run-time cost. Reflection inspects classes while the program runs.

v.q: Why does MapStruct usually start faster than a reflection-based mapper?
o: It generates plain mapping code at compile time
It caches reflection results on disk between runs
It maps only public fields
It runs the mapping on a separate thread
v.w: An annotation processor writes ordinary Java during compilation, so there is no reflection, no lookup and no run-time cost.

v.q: What happens on Java 17 when a library calls setAccessible(true) on a private field of a JDK internal class?
o: It throws InaccessibleObjectException unless the package is opened with --add-opens
It works, but the JVM prints a warning to the log
It works only if the field is also declared final
It is silently ignored, and the field stays private
v.w: Since Java 16 and 17 the JDK's internal packages are strongly encapsulated. The right fix is to update the library.

v.q: Which option correctly gives a library access to a private field of a class in a named JDK module on Java 17?
o: Start the JVM with --add-opens for that package
Call setAccessible(true) twice
Mark the field volatile
Declare the library as a final class
v.w: Strong encapsulation means the module must open the package to the caller. --add-opens is the workaround, and updating the library is the real fix.

v.q: Why do GraalVM native images need extra configuration for reflection?
o: Classes used only through names in strings are invisible to the build-time analysis and would be removed
Native images cannot load any class that has an annotation
Reflection is too slow to be allowed in compiled programs
The native compiler removes every method that is not public
v.w: Native image assumes a closed world and keeps only reachable code. Reflective use must be registered. Spring AOT generates these hints.

v.q: Which statement about reflection in a GraalVM native image is NOT true?
o: Reflection works with no configuration if the class has a public constructor
Reflective use must be registered in hints or config
The closed-world analysis removes code it cannot reach
Spring AOT can generate the hints for you
v.w: Without registration the analysis cannot see classes named only in strings and removes them, whatever their visibility.
